# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Impact
The impact of this finding centers on the PartyGovernanceNFT.sol smart contract, specifically within the context of the burn(uint256 tokenId) function. This critical function operates without any access control mechanisms in place. Consequently, it permits any user, regardless of ownership, to invoke the function and potentially burn someone else's NFTs by supplying the corresponding tokenId. This omission of access control introduces a significant security vulnerability that can have dire consequences.

The potential repercussions of this vulnerability are substantial:

**Unauthorized NFT Destruction:** Malicious users can exploit this oversight to intentionally destroy NFTs owned by other participants in the contract. This act could result in irreversible losses of valuable digital assets.

**Loss of Trust:** Users may lose confidence in the contract's security, affecting the reputation of the platform or service that relies on this contract for NFT governance.

**Financial Implications:** The destruction of NFTs can have financial implications for users who have invested in or depend on the NFTs' functionality. It could lead to legal disputes and financial losses.


## Proof of Concept
Demonstrating by referring to the provided code snippet:

```solidity
function burn(uint256 tokenId) external {
    uint256[] memory tokenIds = new uint256[](1);
    tokenIds[0] = tokenId;
    burn(tokenIds);
}

```

In this code, there are no access control checks to ensure that only the rightful owner of an NFT can burn it. Any user can call this function with a specific tokenId and effectively burn the associated NFT.

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Make sure that only the respective authority can call this function

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-party/blob/main/contracts/party/PartyGovernance.sol#L1097-L1100


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The ragequit functionality is put in place to protect the rights of the minority, who are not in support of a proposal, and allow them to withdraw their share of assets and exit the party.
In some cases, minority will not have the opportunity to ragequit when a proposal will cheat them

## Proof of Concept
Before now, if majority accept a proposal, and the proposal passes, there would be a delay before execution during which host can veto the proposal. During this period, minority can ragequit from the party if proposal does not favour them.

Current changes allow veto period to be skipped once all hosts accept a proposal, but this also means that minority will not have the opportunity to rageQuit if they are not in support of the proposal.

```solidity
function _getProposalStatus(
    ProposalStateValues memory pv
) private view returns (ProposalStatus status) {
    ...
    if (_hostsAccepted(pv.numHosts, pv.numHostsAccepted)) {      
        return ProposalStatus.Ready;
    }
    ...
}
```

This allows host(s) + majority to cheat minority.

In addition, as was reported in another issue, all hosts may not accept a proposal, but a single host can maliciously increase the numHostsAccepted count for a proposal. So this means that: "A SINGLE HOST + MAJORITY CAN EXECUTE A PROPOSAL, GIVING NO CHANCE FOR MINORITY+OTHER HOSTS TO RAGEQUIT"

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Even when all hosts accept a proposal, let there be a brief delay to allow minority to ragequit

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-party/blob/main/contracts/crowdfund/ETHCrowdfundBase.sol#L379
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-party/blob/main/contracts/crowdfund/ETHCrowdfundBase.sol#L333


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
ETHCrowdfundBase#_finalize assumes that all contributions are intact, but there is an emergencyExecute function that is capable of spending part of crowdfund eth. If as little as one wei gets spent, Users cannot get refunded, and the Crowdfund will not get finalized, leading to locking of all contributions. The contract also lacks a receive() callback, which prevents direct transfer of eth to the contract.

## Proof of Concept
There is an [`emergencyExecute`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-party/blob/main/contracts/crowdfund/ETHCrowdfundBase.sol#L379) in ETHCrowdfundBase which allows party DAO to execute an arbitrary function with native value from the contract.

If the DAO spends any amount (as little as 1 wei) from the contract, the address(this).balance will become lower than `totalContributions`.

So `ETHCrowdfundBase#_finalize` will fail because it tries to [transfer](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-party/blob/main/contracts/crowdfund/ETHCrowdfundBase.sol#L333) `totalContributions`, which is greater than the contract's balance.

This means that all the contributions will be forever locked in the contract, as there is also no receive() fallback that can be used to directly send the amount spent to make `finalize` possible.


## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider implementing any of these:
- ETHCrowdfundBase should have a receive() callback
- Instead of transferring totalContributions, finalize should transfer `address(this).balance` or `min(totalContributions,address(this).balance)`

ETH-Transfer

# Vulnerability details

# Bug Description
The recent implementation update empowers the authority to decrease the `totalVotingPower` arbitrarily using the `decreaseTotalVotingPower()` function. This authority-exclusive function allows the reduction of `totalVotingPower` by a specified amount.

One of the main invariants of the governance logic is, that at any time, besides the minting of party cards for the initial crowdfund, `totalVotingPower >= mintedVotingPower`.  This is done because the decision if a vote has passed is done based upon (simplified) dividing the amount of votes by the `totalVotingPower` and checking if that percentage is above the percentage set as the voting threshold. So if `totalVotingPower` exceeds `mintedVotingPower` it leads to the voting system not working as intended. 

The issue arises as the `decreaseTotalVotingPower()` function lacks a check to prevent the new `totalVotingPower` from falling below `mintedVotingPower`. If the authority inadvertently decreases `totalVotingPower` too much, users or groups without majority voting power could pass proposals. If the `totalVotingPower` is reduced to a value less than the voting power of a single user or group, they could unanimously pass proposals, bypassing the veto period where hosts could otherwise prevent the proposal execution.

If the authority unintentionally reduces `totalVotingPower` below `mintedVotingPower`, users or groups lacking sufficient votes to pass a proposal gain the ability to pass proposals at will. This allows malicious users to perform various harmful actions, such as adding themselves as authorities through the `AddAuthorityProposal` and subsequently using the `burn()` function to remove all other users from the party. # Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details
Each proposal state  tracks users that accepted proposal , ensuring that no user can vote more than once. This is necessary because each account is only allowed to vote once on a proposal. However, users have the option to delegate their voting power or transfer their party NFT to another account, and vote the proposal with new account using transferred voting power.

## Impact
Users have the ability to access unlimited voting power.

1- User A possesses a voting power of 100 and gives their approval to a proposal.
2- User A either transfers their party NFT card or delegates their voting power to another address.
3- User A employs a new address to once again approve the proposal and use their voting power again.

Implement a mechanism that safeguards against using voting power of a nft multiple times on same proposal.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-party/blob/b23c65d62a20921c709582b0b76b387f2bb9ebb5/contracts/party/PartyGovernanceNFT.sol#L393


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The ragequit function uses a fixed precision of 1e18 for the calculation of withrawamounts, but not all erc20's precision are equal to 1e18. For example, the precision of `USDC` token is only 1e6.
Suppose a user uses `USDC` token as withrawtokens, and the statement for calculating withrawamounts is as follows:

```solidity
withdrawAmounts[i] += (balance * getVotingPowerShareOf(tokenIds[j])) / 1e18;
```

It can be seen from the formula that it should have been divided by `1e6`, but now it has been divided by `1e18`. The calculation error is very large! The user will get fewer tokens than the actual one.
## Proof of Concept
The code calculated with fixed precision is in line 393 of the `ragequit` function:
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-party/blob/b23c65d62a20921c709582b0b76b387f2bb9ebb5/contracts/party/PartyGovernanceNFT.sol#L393

```solidity
withdrawAmounts[i] += (balance * getVotingPowerShareOf(tokenIds[j])) / 1e18;
```

## Tools Used
Visual Studio Code
Foundry 

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider using the following optimization code:

```solidity
uint256 decimals = address(withdrawTokens[i]) == ETH_ADDRESS ? 1e18 : IERC20(withdrawTokens[i]).decimals();
withdrawAmounts[i] += (balance * getVotingPowerShareOf(tokenIds[j])) /decimals;
```



## Assessed type

Decimal

A party may not be able to close it's lending position fast enough, even though the proposal to do so was approved, and end up liquidated because certain member may front-run other members execute a proposal that leaves the party in a proposal in-progress state.[2]

Unintended collisions can lead to data integrity issues, where different sets of input data produce the same packed representation. This can result in unexpected behavior when decoding the data.

If the packed data is used in security-critical operations such as access control or cryptographic functions, collisions could introduce vulnerabilities and compromise the security of the contract.

Detect collision due to dynamic type usages in `abi.encodePacked`.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The protocol offers enhanced functionality and flexibility to trusted actors (hosts) via the use of trusted smart contracts called authorities.

`PartyGovernanceNFT#increaseTotalVotingPower()` is one such function which is exclusively available to authorities. As the name implies, it is used to increase the total voting power of the party.

An authority which leverages that function is `AddPartyCardsAuthority`. It is an authority which atomically distributes new party cards and updates the total voting power as needed.

A malicious actor can front-run `AddPartyCardsAuthority` which calls `increaseTotalVotingPower()` and `rageQuit()` by taking more funds out of the Party than the rest of the users would be able to.

# Vulnerability details

The `Implementation` contract is designed to be a base class for contracts that are deployed for later use behind a proxy. They provide an `onlyDelegateCall` and an `onlyInitialize` modifier to decorate the implementation functions to make sure they are called properly, that is behind a proxy for the former, and only once for the latter.

The `onlyInitialize` modifier used by the contracts in scope to decorate the initializer functions is however insufficient to secure them, because the implementation contracts can be initialized by anyone without passing by a proxy. While this often does not pose a threat, it sometimes does, especially for contracts whose initializers contain a `delegatecall`. This is the case for `PartyGovernanceNFT` and its children, where risk is however mitigated by the fact for this attack to work, the caller needs to have authority on the `Globals` contract.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-party/blob/main/contracts/signature-validators/OffChainSignatureValidator.sol#L53


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
This new upgrade of the Party protocol allows for Parties to verify offchain signatures over arbitrary data like popular intent based orders or the common "Sign in with Ethereum" message scheme. Parties can choose to assign a custom Signature Validator to a specific message hash by executing a `SetSignatureValidatorProposal`. However in the absense of a custom Signature Validator, the default `OffChainSignatureValidator` is used. This default implementation is vulnerable to replay attacks across different Party instances as it does not enforce that the signed message specificially targets one single Party.

The `OffChainSignatureValidator` verifies that a message was signed by a signer who is
1. a Party member, and
2. has voting power over the signingThreshold for that party

As Party members often belong to multiple Party instances, this implementation is vulnerable to replay attacks. For instance, if a user signs a message for one Party, it can be replayed on other Party instances where that user is also a member.

This has large implications as it undermines the security assumptions that contracts have when verifying 1271 signatures made by Party contracts. Anything from impersonation to loss of funds is possible, depending on what the signed message is used for.

Additionally, while `OffChainSignatureValidator` does not accept 712-signed data, if it is used as a reference for future custom SignatureValidators (ex. for Seaport / UniswapX orders / token approvals), signature replay attacks in those cases can have serious consequences: relayed orders, stolen funds, etc.

While this can be *somewhat* mitigated by integrations adding nonces or other unique data points into the message, there are many existing protocols who do not implement such protections (or rely on other security assumptions).
